questions.scenario: A telecom's customer support agent uses two MCP tools owned by different backend teams. `lookup_customer(query)` is described as "Finds a customer." and `find_account(query)` as "Finds an account record." `lookup_customer` expects an email address; `find_account` expects a 10-digit account number and returns billing status. Logs show 22% of calls send an email to `find_account` or an account number to `lookup_customer`, each followed by a "not found" reply to the customer. The two teams cannot merge the tools this quarter. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add `input_examples` to both tools, one with an email for `lookup_customer` and one with a 10-digit number for `find_account`, so Claude sees the expected formats.
Add a routing rule to the system prompt: "If the customer gives an email, use lookup_customer; if they give an account number, use find_account."
Rewrite both descriptions to state what each tool returns, the exact input format it accepts, when to use it, and when to use the other tool instead.
Rename the tools to `customer_lookup_by_email` and `account_lookup_by_number` and leave the descriptions as they are, since the names now carry the format.
questions.why_correct: Las descripciones son el mecanismo principal con el que el modelo elige tools, y la doc dice que son por lejos el factor más importante. Una buena descripción explica qué hace, cuándo usarla (y cuándo no), qué significa cada parámetro y sus límites. Decir el formato de entrada y nombrar la tool alternativa elimina el solapamiento.

why_wrong.0: Casi: los ejemplos ayudan con el formato, pero la doc los plantea como complemento de una buena descripción, no reemplazo. Con "Finds a customer." sigue sin quedar claro qué devuelve cada una ni cuándo NO usarla.
why_wrong.1: Funcionaría a medias: es una regla aparte que puede chocar con otras instrucciones y no viaja con la tool. El problema está en las descripciones, y ahí se arregla.
why_wrong.3: Renombrar ayuda, pero la guía del examen combina renombrar CON actualizar la descripción; con una línea vaga, el modelo sigue sin saber qué devuelve cada una.

questions.rule: Tools parecidas: descripción con qué hace, formato de entrada, qué devuelve, cuándo sí y cuándo usar la otra.
questions.source_quote: Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance.

questions.scenario: An insurance company's support agent has an `escalate_case` tool with parameters `case_id` and `severity` (`"low" | "medium" | "high"`, required). The tool description says "Escalates a case." and `severity` has no description. In development, 9% of calls omitted `severity`, so a developer enabled strict tool use; now every call includes it, but 41% of escalations for minor billing typos are marked `high`, flooding the on-call queue. The model cannot be changed. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Keep strict tool use and add `"default": "low"` to the `severity` property in the schema, so that unclear cases are assigned the least disruptive value.
Expand the tool and parameter descriptions to define what each severity level means, with concrete criteria and examples of cases that belong in each one.
Turn off strict tool use and validate `severity` in the backend, returning an error so that Claude retries the call whenever the field is missing.
Split `escalate_case` into three tools, `escalate_low`, `escalate_medium`, and `escalate_high`, so the model chooses the severity by choosing the tool.
questions.why_correct: Si Claude usa mal una tool (por ejemplo, le faltan parámetros), suele ser porque no tenía información suficiente para usarla bien; la doc recomienda volver a probar con `description` más detalladas. Strict garantiza la FORMA (el campo siempre está), no el criterio para elegir el valor. Definir qué es cada nivel ataca la causa.

why_wrong.0: Un default no le explica al modelo cuándo un caso es alto; strict ya hace que lo complete, y seguiría eligiendo `high` sin criterio.
why_wrong.2: Vuelve al síntoma original (campo faltante) y suma reintentos, sin darle al modelo el criterio que le falta.
why_wrong.3: Multiplica tools casi idénticas: más ambigüedad de selección, y la decisión de severidad sigue sin criterio documentado.

questions.rule: Strict asegura el formato; el criterio para elegir valores lo da la descripción.
questions.source_quote: The best approach during development is to try the request again with more-detailed `description` values in your tool definitions.

questions.scenario: An online retailer's support agent first calls `search_orders(email)`, which returns objects like `{"order_number": "A-48213", "order_uuid": "5f2c…", "status": "shipped"}`. It then calls `cancel_order(order_id)` when customers ask to cancel. The `cancel_order` description is "Cancels an order." and `order_id` is described as "The order ID." Logs show 35% of cancellations fail with `order not found`, because Claude passes the customer-facing `A-48213` instead of the UUID. The API cannot change this sprint. What is the best fix?
options: Describe `order_id` as the `order_uuid` field returned by `search_orders`, not the customer-facing `order_number`, and say in the tool description it must follow a search.
Add an `input_examples` entry to `cancel_order` with a sample UUID, so Claude learns from the example that the parameter is a UUID rather than an order number.
Add `"pattern"` with a UUID regex to `order_id` in the schema, so the API rejects calls with an order number before they reach the cancellation backend.
Add a system prompt rule telling Claude to never show `order_uuid` values to customers and to always pass them, not order numbers, to any tool.
questions.why_correct: La doc pide explicar qué significa cada parámetro y cómo afecta el comportamiento. Acá el parámetro tiene una relación con otra tool: viene del campo `order_uuid` de `search_orders`. Decirlo en la descripción resuelve el formato Y de dónde sale el valor, que es lo que el modelo no sabía.

why_wrong.1: Casi: el ejemplo muestra el formato, pero no dice que el valor sale de `order_uuid` en el resultado de `search_orders`. La doc dice que los ejemplos complementan; la descripción es lo primero.
why_wrong.2: Convierte un error de negocio en un error de validación, pero el modelo sigue sin saber cuál campo usar: trata el síntoma.
why_wrong.3: Es una regla global, lejos de la tool, y mezcla dos cosas (privacidad y formato). La información pertenece a la descripción del parámetro.

questions.rule: Si un parámetro sale de otra tool, decí de cuál y de qué campo en su descripción.
questions.source_quote: What each parameter means and how it affects the tool’s behavior

questions.scenario: A developer-productivity team connected an internal `codesearch` MCP server to Claude Code. Its `search_symbols` tool queries a semantic index across 140 repositories, including ones not cloned locally, and returns definitions, callers, and owning teams. Its description is "Searches code." Developers on Windows ask questions like "Who calls `PaymentGateway.charge` across the company?", and in 80% of sessions Claude uses the built-in Grep on the current repository only, missing most callers. The team does not want to disable Grep, which is useful for local edits. What should they change?
options: Add a `permissions.deny` rule for `Grep` in the project settings, so Claude has to use `search_symbols` for any search across the code base.
Add a line to `CLAUDE.md` asking Claude to prefer the `codesearch` MCP server over built-in tools whenever a question involves other repositories.
Set `alwaysLoad: true` on the `codesearch` server, so its tool definitions are always in context and Claude considers them before the built-in tools.
Expand the `search_symbols` description to explain that it covers all 140 repositories, returns callers and owners, and when to use it instead of local search.
questions.why_correct: La guía del examen lo plantea textual: mejorar las descripciones de las tools MCP explicando en detalle capacidades y salidas, para que el agente no prefiera tools built-in (como `Grep`) sobre tools MCP más capaces. Con "Searches code." el modelo no tiene cómo saber que cubre 140 repos y devuelve callers.

why_wrong.0: Rompe el uso local de `Grep` que el equipo quiere mantener. Es enforcement donde el problema es de información.
why_wrong.1: Ayuda algo, pero es guidance lejos de la tool; la descripción sigue sin decir qué hace la tool, que es lo que el modelo usa para elegir.
why_wrong.2: Que la definición esté cargada no sirve si la definición dice "Searches code.": el modelo la ve y sigue sin saber que es mejor que `Grep`.

questions.rule: Si el agente prefiere `Grep` a tu tool MCP, tu descripción no está contando lo que la tool hace mejor.
questions.source_quote: Enhancing MCP tool descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs in detail, preventing the agent from preferring built-in tools (like Grep) over more capable MCP tools

questions.scenario: A subscription company's support agent uses `get_customer(customer_id)`, described as "Returns the customer's profile and account details." It returns name, plan, and address, but not payment methods, which live in `get_payment_methods(customer_id)`. When customers ask "Which card will you charge?", the agent calls `get_customer`, finds no card, and in 12% of cases states a card that doesn't exist, such as "your Visa ending in 4242." QA wants the agent to stop inventing card details. Which change best addresses why the agent picks the wrong tool?
options: Add `payment_methods` to the `get_customer` response with a null value, so the agent sees explicitly that the field is empty and stops filling it in.
Add to the system prompt that the agent must never mention card details unless they appear verbatim in a tool result returned in the same turn.
State in `get_customer`'s description that it does not return payment methods and that `get_payment_methods` should be used for cards and billing details.
Merge both tools into `get_customer(customer_id, include)` with an `include` enum, so the agent requests the payment methods in the same call.
questions.why_correct: La doc pide incluir en la descripción las advertencias y límites, como qué información NO devuelve la tool. "Account details" sugiere que incluye pagos; aclarar que no y apuntar a `get_payment_methods` arregla la elección de tool, que es lo que causa el invento.

why_wrong.0: Ayuda a no inventar en esa respuesta, pero el agente sigue eligiendo la tool equivocada y no llega a los datos reales de la tarjeta.
why_wrong.1: Ataca el síntoma (inventar) pero no la causa (elegir mal la tool): el cliente sigue sin su respuesta.
why_wrong.3: Consolidar es una práctica válida en general, pero no es la causa raíz acá: con `include` mal documentado, el agente puede seguir sin pedir los pagos. Y requiere cambiar el backend.

questions.rule: Decí en la descripción qué NO devuelve la tool y cuál sí lo devuelve.
questions.source_quote: Any important caveats or limitations, such as what information the tool does not return if the tool name is unclear.

questions.scenario: A consulting firm's multi-agent research system gives its search subagent two MCP tools: `analyze_content(query)`, which searches the public web and summarizes results, and `analyze_document(query)`, which searches the firm's internal knowledge base of client deliverables. Their descriptions are "Analyzes content for the query." and "Analyzes documents for the query." In an audit of 300 reports, 27% of findings about the firm's own methodology came from public blog posts, while questions about competitors' announcements sometimes returned only internal slides. The tools' backends work correctly. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add a coordinator step that classifies each question as internal or external and passes the classification to the subagent before it chooses a tool.
Rename them to `search_public_web` and `search_internal_kb`, with descriptions stating each one's source, what it returns, and when to use the other instead.
Keep the names and expand both descriptions to four sentences each, describing in detail how the analysis and summarization of results is performed.
Merge both into a single `analyze(query, source)` tool with a `source` enum of `web` or `internal`, so the subagent has only one tool to choose.
questions.why_correct: Nombres y descripciones casi idénticos (el ejemplo de la guía es justo `analyze_content` vs. `analyze_document`) causan misrouting. La guía recomienda renombrar para eliminar el solapamiento y actualizar las descripciones con el propósito, las entradas, las salidas y cuándo usar cada una frente a la alternativa.

why_wrong.0: Agrega un paso y costo para compensar descripciones malas: trata el síntoma.
why_wrong.2: Más largas, pero describen lo que tienen EN COMÚN (analizar y resumir) y no lo que las distingue: la fuente. El largo no reemplaza los límites.
why_wrong.3: Consolidar puede servir, pero con `source` sin documentar el subagente vuelve a la misma decisión ambigua, solo que en un parámetro.

questions.rule: Tools con nombres y descripciones parecidas → renombrá por función y escribí los límites entre ellas.
questions.source_quote: Renaming tools and updating descriptions to eliminate functional overlap (e.g., renaming analyze_content to extract_web_results with a web-specific description)

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company's support agent has well-written tool descriptions: `search_policies` for general store policies and `get_order` for the details and eligibility of a specific order. Last month someone added this line to the system prompt: "Whenever the customer mentions a policy, refund, or return, search the policies first." Since then, for messages like "Can I return order 88172? It arrived broken," the agent calls `search_policies` and answers with generic rules in 46% of cases, without checking the order's actual eligibility. Tool descriptions were not changed. What should the team do first?
options: Add `input_examples` to `get_order` showing order numbers taken from return requests, so Claude associates return messages that cite an order with that tool.
Expand the `get_order` description to say it must be used for any message that mentions an order number, including returns and refunds of that order.
Review the system prompt and rewrite the keyword-triggered instruction so it no longer forces `search_policies` whenever certain words appear in a message.
Rename `search_policies` to `search_general_policies` so its name no longer matches the words "policy", "refund", and "return" in customer messages.
questions.why_correct: La guía del examen marca este caso: instrucciones del system prompt sensibles a palabras clave pueden crear asociaciones no buscadas con tools y pisar descripciones bien escritas. Las descripciones no cambiaron; el problema empezó con esa línea. Primero se revisa y corrige el prompt.

why_wrong.0: Agrega señales a una tool que ya estaba bien descrita, compitiendo contra una orden explícita del prompt.
why_wrong.1: Mejora la descripción, pero el prompt sigue ordenando "buscá las políticas primero": la instrucción explícita sigue ganando.
why_wrong.3: El disparador es la palabra del cliente en el prompt, no el nombre de la tool; renombrar no saca la instrucción.

questions.rule: Si una tool bien descrita igual se elige mal, revisá el system prompt buscando reglas por palabra clave.
questions.source_quote: Reviewing system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that might override well-written tool descriptions

questions.scenario: A SaaS company's internal assistant, built on the API with tool search enabled, has 260 tools from GitHub, Jira, Slack, and PagerDuty integrations. Several services expose tools named `search`, `list_items`, and `get_item`, each with a decent description that doesn't mention the service. Logs show that for "find the Jira ticket about the login outage," tool search loads GitHub and Slack `search` tools 31% of the time, and Claude then searches the wrong system. Disabling tool search is not an option because of the context budget. Which change most directly fixes the selection?
options: Prefix every tool name with its service, such as `jira_search` and `github_search`, and make each description state which system and records it searches.
Consolidate each service's tools into a single tool per service with an `action` parameter, so there are only four tools left for tool search to choose from.
Mark the Jira tools to always load upfront, since Jira questions are the most common ones and loading them first avoids the confusion with other services.
Add one `input_examples` entry per tool with a realistic query for its service, so tool search matches requests against the examples as well.
questions.why_correct: La doc recomienda namespacing con el prefijo del servicio (`github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`) cuando las tools cruzan varios servicios: hace la selección inequívoca a medida que crece la biblioteca, y es especialmente importante con tool search. Sumado a descripciones que digan qué sistema buscan, la búsqueda deja de mezclar.

why_wrong.1: Consolidar es una buena práctica en general, pero con 260 tools de cuatro servicios tendrías tools gigantes y descripciones largas: el problema puntual es la ambigüedad entre servicios, que resuelve el namespacing.
why_wrong.2: Resuelve un servicio y gasta contexto en cada turno; las búsquedas en GitHub o Slack siguen confundiéndose.
why_wrong.3: La doc no dice que tool search busque en `input_examples`; y los nombres siguen siendo iguales entre servicios.

questions.rule: Tools de varios servicios: prefijo por servicio en el nombre (más importante con tool search).
questions.source_quote: When your tools span multiple services or resources, prefix names with the service (for example, `github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`). This makes tool selection unambiguous as your library grows, and is especially important when using tool search.

questions.scenario: A research organization's fact-checking pipeline gives an agent one MCP tool, `analyze_document(doc_id, instructions)`, described as "Analyzes a document according to the instructions." The agent uses it for three different jobs: pulling figures into a table, summarizing sections, and checking whether a claim is supported by a source. Outputs are inconsistent: 18% of claim checks return a summary instead of a verdict, and downstream code fails to parse them because each job needs a different output shape. The team controls the server. What design change addresses this?
options: Keep the single tool but add an `output_format` enum parameter with `table`, `summary`, and `verdict` values, documented in the tool's description.
Keep the single tool and add three `input_examples`, one per job, showing the instructions and expected output so Claude learns each pattern.
Keep the single tool and post-process its output with a classifier that detects which job was intended and reformats the result into the expected shape.
Split it into `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, and `verify_claim_against_source`, each with a description and a defined input/output contract.
questions.why_correct: La guía del examen tiene este ejemplo exacto: partir una tool genérica `analyze_document` en tools con propósito específico (`extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, `verify_claim_against_source`) con contratos de entrada y salida definidos. Cada tool tiene una descripción que dice para qué sirve, y la salida de cada una tiene forma fija.

why_wrong.0: Casi: un enum ayuda, pero la tool sigue siendo genérica, su contrato de salida depende de un parámetro, y la descripción tiene que explicar tres trabajos a la vez.
why_wrong.1: Los ejemplos de input no fijan el formato de salida; y la tool sigue sin propósito claro.
why_wrong.2: Repara después lo que salió mal antes: trata el síntoma y suma otra pieza que puede fallar.

questions.rule: Una tool genérica que hace muchas cosas → varias tools con propósito y contrato propio.
questions.source_quote: Splitting generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts

questions.scenario: An accounts-payable platform extracts data from uploaded documents with the Messages API. Each request offers two extraction tools, `extract_invoice` and `extract_receipt`, with `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}`. Descriptions are "Extracts invoice data." and "Extracts receipt data." On a labeled set of 2,000 documents, 18% of receipts (proof of a completed payment, no due date) are sent to `extract_invoice`, which then returns `null` for its required-in-practice `due_date` and `invoice_number`. Cost rules allow only one API call per document. What is the most effective change?
options: Switch to `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_receipt"}` for documents under one page, since most receipts are short and invoices are usually longer.
Add a separate classification call before extraction, and force the matching extraction tool with `tool_choice` set to the tool chosen in the first call.
Make `due_date` and `invoice_number` required in the `extract_invoice` schema, so the model can't choose that tool for a document that lacks those fields.
Rewrite both descriptions to state the document characteristics each one covers, such as a payment request with a due date versus proof of a completed payment.
questions.why_correct: Con `tool_choice: any` el modelo elige entre las dos tools según sus descripciones. "Extracts invoice data." no le dice qué distingue una factura de un recibo. Describir las características de cada documento y cuándo NO usar cada tool corrige la selección dentro de la misma llamada, respetando el costo.

why_wrong.0: Una heurística por largo que la API no conoce: va a forzar facturas cortas al extractor de recibos.
why_wrong.1: Funciona, y forzar con `tool_choice` es legítimo, pero son dos llamadas por documento: viola la regla de costo.
why_wrong.2: Hacerlos obligatorios no impide elegir la tool: empuja al modelo a inventar fecha y número para cumplir el schema. Es el principio de "el modelo inventa datos".

questions.rule: Con `tool_choice: any`, lo que decide cuál tool es la descripción: escribí qué la distingue de la otra.
questions.source_quote: When it should be used (and when it shouldn’t)

questions.scenario: A furniture retailer's support agent has `update_customer_profile(customer_id, fields)`, described as "Updates customer information such as name, phone, and address." and `update_shipping_address(order_id, address)`, described as "Changes where an order ships." When customers ask to send an already-placed order to a new address, the agent calls `update_customer_profile` in 29% of cases, which only changes the default for future orders; the order ships to the old address. Both tools work as designed and must stay separate because they write to different systems. Which change most directly prevents this misrouting?
options: Remove `address` from the fields `update_customer_profile` accepts, so the agent can no longer change any address through the profile tool at all.
State in `update_customer_profile`'s description that it doesn't affect orders already placed, and that `update_shipping_address` changes an existing order's destination.
Add a post-call check that compares the customer's open orders with the new profile address and warns the agent when a placed order still has the old address.
Add `input_examples` to `update_shipping_address` showing an order id and a new address, so Claude recognizes requests about a specific order more often.
questions.why_correct: Las dos descripciones hablan de "address" sin marcar el límite entre ellas. La práctica documentada es que la descripción diga cuándo usar la tool y cuándo no, y sus limitaciones. Aclarar que el perfil no toca pedidos ya hechos y nombrar la tool correcta para ese caso corta el misrouting en la elección.

why_wrong.0: Rompe un uso legítimo (cambiar la dirección por defecto) para tapar un problema de descripción.
why_wrong.2: Detecta el error después de cometerlo: trata el síntoma y suma llamadas.
why_wrong.3: Ayuda con el formato de la otra tool, pero no dice que el perfil NO cambia pedidos existentes, que es la confusión real.

questions.rule: En tools que se pisan, la descripción marca la frontera: qué no hace y qué tool hace eso.
questions.source_quote: The more context you can give Claude about your tools, the better it will be at determining when and how to use them.
